transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Zephyr Head of AI), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead), Sofia Ruiz (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on per-token economics, how caching and batching affect unit cost and tail latency, and initial feasibility of Hosted vs Dedicated for a retail personalization use case. Customer had strong constraints on 95th/99th latency and a fixed monthly inference budget.

Topics:
- Current token volumes and peak QPS
- Latency SLOs (95th and 99th)
- Cost tradeoffs: hosted per-token vs reserved dedicated
- Caching (prefix / KV cache) and batching strategies
- Privacy / VPC and compliance considerations

Action items summary (captured): see action_items field above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, i'm Avery from Redwood, i'll run the intro, we've got Diego from infra who will go into latency and cache mechanics. um quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya: maya here — hi.
[00:09] Liam: liam here.
[00:11] Sofia: sofia here.
[00:13] Avery: awesome. quick agenda: understand your workload (tokens, qps), what latency you need, and whether hosted, dedicated or private makes sense cost-wise. sound good?
[00:22] Maya: yea, we'll be quick. high level — we're building personalized product recommendations embedded in the checkout flow, so latency is pretty sensitive. 95th under 200ms ideally, 99th under 400ms if possible. monthly tokens projected at 1.2B to start, seasonal peaks up to 2.5B.
[00:40] Diego: thank you. couple clarifying q's — when you say tokens, is that input+output tokens combined, or just the generated tokens?
[00:46] Maya: both combined. our telemetry now counts both sides. approx ratio 70% input, 30% output per request.
[00:52] Diego: got it. and concurrency? peak qps?
[00:55] Liam: on peak days, we see 350 qps sustained for 10-15 minute bursts, outside of that baseline is ~40 qps.
[01:03] Diego: good, that helps. so rough math — hosted per-token pricing will be simple to model but tail latencies can be higher depending on shared fleet and coldpop issues; dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and more consistent p95/p99 but you pay commitment.
[01:18] Avery: maybe i'll interrupt — quick numbers: for our typical LLMs in the catalogue, hosted is around $X per 1M input+output tokens for the 16k context family; dedicated effectively reduces unit cost by 20-50% depending on utilization and batching. those are rough, we'll send exact numbers.
[01:33] Sofia: can you speak to the batching side? is it transparent on hosted? we can't change client behavior in checkout, so per-request latency is critical.
[01:40] Diego: good question. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching, but batching is a trade: more batching increases throughput and lowers per-token cost, but it adds waiting time while the batch fills. for a checkout flow where each request wants immediate response, batching window must be very tight — say 2-5ms — which limits effective batch size. you can still get some micro-batches from concurrent qps, but not the big cost wins you see in async workloads.
[02:04] Maya: so given our 350 qps bursts, does that mean batching helps during peaks?
[02:08] Diego: yes, during bursts you'll see natural batching and better GPU utilization. we've seen effective batch sizes of 8-32 during spikes which materially drops cost. at baseline 40 qps, batch sizes are small so less benefit.
[02:18] Liam: what about caching? our prompts have a lot of shared prefix — product catalog context and user segmentation — maybe we can cache those.
[02:25] Diego: caching is where you can reclaim both cost and latency. two levers: prefix caching (server-side reuse of repeated prompt prefixes) and KV-style hidden-state caching (we call it KV cache, sometimes transcribed as KV cash in the notes), which stores model key/value activations for previously seen contexts. prefix cache reduces tokenization cost and avoids re-sending the same context; KV cache reduces computation at decode time. both reduce latency and token compute.
[02:46] Maya: curious about cache hit rates we should aim for. is 50% hit rate realistic?
[02:50] Diego: for product recommendation flows with templated catalog data, 60-80% prefix hit is realistic if you normalize prompts. KV cache hit depends on how often the same user-context repeats; with session-level repeats you can see 30-50% KV hits. overall hit rate is workload dependent; we'll ask for sample logs.
[03:05] Avery: and important — cache TTLs, eviction, privacy. if you're in hosted, cache is managed by Redwood and respects retention config; in private/V P C deployments you control eviction and keys. for PCI-related data, you'd likely want to keep sensitive tokens out of cache or use customer-managed key encryption.
[03:24] Sofia: we do have PCI and need to keep PII out of model inputs — can we redact and still get cache benefits?
[03:30] Diego: yes, best practice is deterministic redaction or placeholders — replace user-specific info with stable tokens before caching. that preserves cacheability while protecting PII. there is a small quality tradeoff but usually acceptable.
[03:41] Maya: back to price math — can you walk through an example per-request cost with and without caching/batching?
[03:47] Avery: sure. quick example, assume 150 tokens total per request, monthly 1.2B tokens. hosted nominal price let's say $0.40 per 1k tokens (placeholder); that yields $480k / month. with 30% effective reduction due to caching and batching combined, you're down to ~$336k. dedicated, with 65% utilization and reserved capacity, could bring unit cost down another 25-35% compared to hosted net, so potentially $220k/month. again we will send real model-specific numbers.
[04:23] Liam: those hosted numbers feel high vs our internal model runs. what's in the hosted price? is it model size, context length?
[04:29] Avery: hosted pricing is model family-specific; larger context/longer generation increases cost. also hidden is the operational premium for multi-tenant reliability, autoscaling, and data-plane throughput. we can break out per-token for input vs output and show quantized model variants.
[04:44] Maya: how do fallbacks work? if p99 spikes, do you route to a smaller model automatically?
[04:49] Diego: yes — smart routing policies can fallback to cheaper/shorter models by rule or on latency thresholds. Redwood has automated fallback that keeps clients within latency SLOs at slight quality regression. you can also do canary rollouts and gradual traffic shifting.
[05:01] Sofia: about private deployment — if we go V P C or on-prem, do you still have automatic batching and caching?
[05:07] Diego: yes, the runtime is consistent across hosted, dedicated, and private. the difference is control: private gives you network isolation and customer-managed keys; dedicated gives reserved GPUs but still a Redwood control plane unless you opt for the private control plane add-on.
[05:21] Liam: what about SLA? we need 99.9% availability during business hours for checkout. is that possible on hosted?
[05:27] Avery: hosted can give strong SLAs on enterprise plans, but the firm SLA for 99.9% often comes with Dedicated or Private with reserved capacity + support. we should map your traffic windows and talk through commit levels.
[05:38] Maya: ok, so practical POC ask — we'd like a 2-week POC that demonstrates per-token cost reduction with prefix normalization + KV-cache, and shows p95/p99 latency under load at our expected peak. is that feasible?
[05:50] Diego: absolutely. typical POCs include a loading script for your QPS pattern, a baseline run (no cache, minimal batching) and an optimized run with normalization, caching, and batching settings. we'll capture token counts, GPU utilization, and latency percentiles.
[06:02] Liam: question — do you support throughput tests that inject realistic network jitter, since our retail systems see CDN variance?
[06:08] Diego: yes we can run tests from multiple regions or simulate added network latency; that will help capture tail behaviour. we often present p50/p95/p99 and tail sample traces.
[06:16] Sofia: what about observability — we need token-level cost breakdown for routes and per-user tracing for debugging.
[06:22] Avery: Redwood Console shows token and cost breakdown per route, per model; you can instrument request IDs and see traces. for PII, we mask in logs unless you opt-in.
[06:31] Maya: what's the implementation lift for dedicated vs hosted POC? timeline wise?
[06:36] Avery: hosted POC is fastest — 1-2 days to get keys and routes, tests can start same week. Dedicated requires capacity reservation and a slightly longer provisioning — usually 2-3 weeks depending on commit. Private/VPC adds network and security review time. given your PCI requirements, we can run an initial hosted POC with strict redaction and then discuss dedicated/private for production.
[06:56] Liam: on encryption — we want KMS integration and customer-managed keys for any cached artifacts; is that supported on hosted?
[07:03] Diego: hosted supports envelope encryption and Redwood-managed keys by default; for CMK you can use dedicated/private with KMS integration. we can also provide an audit trail for cache access and key usage in enterprise plans.
[07:15] Maya: can you send the security doc set? we need SOC 2, ISO, and PCI scoping.
[07:20] Avery: yes — i'll attach the security pack and a redacted sample of audit logs.
[07:24] Sofia: during the POC we want to test different cache TTL strategies — short TTL (30s), medium (5m), and session-scoped — to see hit vs staleness. can you support that?
[07:34] Diego: absolutely. we'll parameterize TTL and show hit/miss and quality impact metrics.
[07:39] Maya: one more — on-model quantization or smaller model variants for cost: how much quality loss should we expect if we move from base to 8-bit quantized variant?
[07:46] Diego: often small regen performance hit for common tasks; careful evals needed. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles by workload — sometimes you get 1-3% metric drop with big cost savings. we'll run evals on your prompt set as part of the POC.
[07:58] Avery: quick recap and next steps?
[08:00] Maya: please send pricing spreadsheet and security docs. we'll share traffic diagrams and sample request logs.
[08:06] Avery: noted. Diego will outline the caching experiment and test plan. we'll target POC kickoff the week of Nov 1 pending internal approvals.
[08:14] Liam: sounds good.
[08:16] Sofia: one last quick question about billing granularity — monthly invoice vs daily usage reporting — we need to tie spend to product teams.
[08:24] Avery: invoicing can be monthly; console gives daily breakdowns and you can pull detailed usage CSVs to push into your chargeback. for Dedicated there's also committed monthly invoice plus true-up.
[08:36] Maya: ok thanks, that's it from our side.
[08:39] Avery: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the items agreed.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions; some acronyms transcribed as separate letters (V P C) and "KV cash" appears in auto notes. The audio had slight background noise at ~minute 30 causing a few words to be garbled.
